title: The synagogue today
hook: synagogues of every size and style, from shtiebels to cathedrals

segments.voice: Yesterday, tikkun olam, from a court in the Mishnah to the food drive, and the line repair the world. Did your one hour get a time and a place? Today, the room where much of Jewish life gathers. Day one thousand fifty-four.

Up a narrow staircase, past a rack of coats, there's a room about the size of a living room. A bookcase bursting with worn volumes. A small cabinet against one wall. Folding chairs that don't match. Men and women are drifting in on a weekday morning, nodding hello. Across town stands a building with a great dome, tall windows and seats for a crowd. And somewhere else, a laptop is open on a kitchen table, with a grid of faces waiting to begin. All three are synagogues. Today: the synagogue, as it is now.
screen: `A ROOM UP A NARROW STAIRCASE.` → `A GREAT DOME ACROSS TOWN.` → `A GRID OF FACES ON A SCREEN.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew, a synagogue is a beit knesset, a house of gathering. That's the heart of it. Not first a building, but people coming together. The Torah sets the pattern when God tells Moses: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." Some readers linger on the last words. Not dwell in it. Among them. Later, the prophet Ezekiel tells the exiles that God will be to the scattered people "as a little sanctuary". The Talmud reads that as the synagogues and houses of study wherever Jews live. A little sanctuary, carried into every land. So what makes one? Not size. The Mishnah says certain parts of the service, like reading the Torah aloud to the congregation, need ten people, a minyan. Nothing there requires a rabbi. A knowledgeable member can lead the prayers. Inside, there's usually an ark holding the Torah scrolls, a lamp kept burning that recalls the lamp in the ancient sanctuary, and a reading table. Synagogues are traditionally built to face Jerusalem. Then the styles spread out. A Hasidic shtiebel, a small room used as a synagogue, full of books, study and prayer. A grand domed building with a choir. A Sephardi synagogue with the reading table in the middle and seats around it. Orthodox synagogues seat men and women separately; Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist synagogues usually seat families together. Some communities meet in a rented hall, a home or online. Each one is a house of gathering in its own way. Today's line: the gathering place.
screen: `BEIT KNESSET: A HOUSE OF GATHERING.` · `DWELL AMONG THEM.` · `A LITTLE SANCTUARY IN EVERY LAND.` · `TEN PEOPLE, AND NO RABBI REQUIRED.` · then, large: `THE GATHERING PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: visit a synagogue, even online. For this sit, start with a gathering you know. Breathe, and bring to mind a room where people you care about come together: a kitchen, a team, a place of worship of any kind. Notice what makes it feel like a gathering place. The faces? The sounds? The way people greet each other at the door? Then think of a synagogue near you, or one that streams its services. Choose a time this week to step in or log on, as a guest who simply wants to see. Calling ahead is a kind thing to do. If you pray, you can pray in your own words for the people who gather there. The bell holds the time.
The synagogue today. A beit knesset, a house of gathering, from a small shtiebel to a domed hall to a screen of faces. Today's word.
Your line: the gathering place. Today, find the website of one synagogue near you, and look at what happens there this week. Day one thousand fifty-four.

howItsDone: Jews gather in synagogues of every size for prayer, Torah reading, study, celebrations and mourning; some prayers need a minyan of ten, services can be led by any knowledgeable member, and some congregations also stream services online.

original.note: Hebrew: a house of gathering, the everyday word for a synagogue.

trapdoor: what you thought: a synagogue is a building with a rabbi in charge.
what it means: a house of gathering of any size or style, where ten people can pray and any knowledgeable member can lead.
what a scholar hears: dwell among them, not in it; Ezekiel's little sanctuary read by the Talmud as the synagogue; the Mishnah's minyan.

notes: Claims rule: no counts; facing Jerusalem stated as tradition ('traditionally built to face Jerusalem'). Please confirm.
Seating: Orthodox separate; Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist 'usually' together. Please confirm.
'Readers have long noticed... not dwell in it, among them' is a well-known homiletic reading (often attributed to later commentators); attributed to 'readers' only.
Megillah 29a reads Ezekiel 11:16 'little sanctuary' as synagogues and houses of study in Babylonia/exile; please confirm. JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 25:8 and the Ezekiel phrase should be checked.
Mishnah Megillah 4:3 lists parts of the service (including public Torah reading) requiring ten. Please confirm.
Ner tamid linked to Exodus 27:20 (the lamp in the Tabernacle); paraphrased. Shtiebel described as 'a small room used as a synagogue' (no etymology given).
